title: "Week 10 Self-Check"
subtitle: "MC 451 · The Sample and the Pilot"
---

Eight questions on this week's terms. **Nothing here is graded and nothing is recorded.** Answer
each question in your head or on paper first, then open the answer under it.

Every term is defined on the slides: [S19, The Sample](../decks/mc451/s19-the-sample.html) and
[S20, The Pilot](../decks/mc451/s20-pilot-kappa-alpha.html). The full explanation is in
[Chapter 10](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v/chapters/chapter10.html).

## 1. What a variable is

Which of these is a **variable** in the example chat study?

- **A.** One chat message from Bob Ross's channel
- **B.** Message target: whether a message speaks to the streamer, to another viewer, or to the whole room
- **C.** The R function `sample_messages()`
- **D.** The week the chat was collected, which is the same for every message

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 1</summary>

**B.** A variable is something about a case that can change from one case to the next. Message
target changes from one message to the next. A is a case, one thing you study. C is a tool. D is
the same for every message, so it does not vary.

</details>

## 2. A category you code

Which of these is a **category you code** yourself, rather than a column already in the data?

- **A.** `viewers`, the viewer count in the stream table
- **B.** `game`, the game a stream was filed under
- **C.** Message target: streamer, another viewer, or the whole room
- **D.** `date`, the date of a stream snapshot

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 2</summary>

**C.** The data already holds `viewers`, `game`, and `date`. Nobody labeled messages by who they
speak to, so you read each message and decide, using the rules in your codebook. That reading and
deciding is what **coding** means.

</details>

## 3. Population and sample

A study is about every message posted in the fifty example channels during one week. You code
thirty messages from each channel. What is the **population**, and what is the **sample**?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 3</summary>

The **population** is every message posted in the fifty channels that week: everything your
conclusions are about. The **sample** is the 1,350 messages you actually code, thirty from each
of the fifty channels, except where a channel had fewer than thirty to give.

</details>

## 4. Biased or representative

You draw 1,000 messages at random from the whole chat table. Almost all of them come from giant
gaming channels, and only one or two come from Bob Ross's channel. Is the sample **biased**? Is it
**representative** of non-gaming chat?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 4</summary>

**Not biased, and not representative.** The draw is unbiased because every message had the same
chance of being picked. It is still not representative of non-gaming chat, because one or two
messages cannot give a fair picture of that group. A sample can avoid one problem and still have
the other.

</details>

## 5. Stratified sampling

Your study compares gaming chat with non-gaming chat. Which draw puts **every** non-gaming channel
in the sample?

- **A.** 1,350 messages drawn at random from the whole chat table
- **B.** Thirty messages drawn from each of the fifty channels
- **C.** 1,350 messages from the busiest channel
- **D.** The first 1,350 messages, in time order

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 5</summary>

**B.** That is **stratified sampling**: split the population into groups (strata), here the
channels, then draw from each group separately. Because every channel is a stratum, every
non-gaming channel is in the sample by construction, not by luck. A would be almost all gaming
chat.

</details>

## 6. The seed

Why does `seed = 409` matter when you draw your sample?

- **A.** 409 is the best number for drawing samples
- **B.** It makes the same random draw come out every time, so anyone can check your work
- **C.** It makes the sample bigger
- **D.** It removes bias from the sample

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 6</summary>

**B.** A **seed** fixes a random draw so it comes out the same on every run. The number itself
means nothing; what matters is that a seed is set and written into your sampling plan. Without it,
nobody can check your results, including you in six months.

</details>

## 7. Independent passes

In your pilot you code the same items twice. Why must your first-pass codes stay hidden until the
second pass is finished?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 7</summary>

The two passes must be **independent**. If you look at your first codes, the second pass measures
your memory, not your codebook's rules. The pilot tests whether the written rules alone give the
same answer, which is why the passes are at least 48 hours apart with the first codes out of
sight.

</details>

## 8. Raw agreement and kappa

Your two passes give the same code on 74 of 100 items, but **Cohen's kappa** comes out at 0.236.
What does that tell you, and what do you do next?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 8</summary>

**Most of the agreement was luck.** Raw agreement was 74 percent, but chance alone would have
produced about 66 percent, so kappa credits the codebook only with the small difference. A kappa
of 0.236 is well under the 0.70 that published work treats as the lowest acceptable value. Go
back to the items your passes coded differently, rewrite each unclear rule, and pilot again on
fresh items.

</details>
